title: Slices: borrowing part of a collection
summary: Refer to a run of elements instead of the whole: string slices (&str), why string literals are slices, array slices (&[T]), and why slices make APIs both safer and more flexible.

blocks.md: A **slice** is a reference to a contiguous run of elements in a collection, rather than the whole collection. Because it is a reference, it does not own anything. This lesson follows *The Rust Programming Language*'s example, a function that finds the first word of a sentence, and shows how slices turn a subtle bug into a compile error.

blocks.title: The problem
blocks.md: Write a function that takes a string of words separated by spaces and returns the first word. Without slices, the best we can return is the **index** where the first word ends:

blocks.explain: `as_bytes` gives the String's bytes; `enumerate` pairs each with its index; `b' '` is the byte for a space. The bug: `word` is just a number with no connection to `s`. After `s.clear()` the number is meaningless, and nothing warns us. Keeping such indexes in sync by hand is fragile.

blocks.title: String slices
blocks.md: A **string slice** is a reference to part of a String, written with a range in brackets:

blocks.explain: `[a..b]` includes `a` and stops before `b`; either end can be left out. Internally a slice stores a pointer to the starting byte and a length, so `world` points at byte 6 of `s` with length 5.

blocks.title: Slice indexes are bytes, not characters
blocks.md: String slice ranges count **bytes** of UTF-8. Slicing in the middle of a multi-byte character, like `&"Здравствуйте"[0..1]` (each Cyrillic letter is 2 bytes), panics with `byte index 1 is not a char boundary`. For ASCII text bytes and characters are the same; chapter 8 shows how to work with characters safely.

blocks.title: first_word, fixed
blocks.md: The type of a string slice is written `&str`. Returning one ties the result to the String it came from:

Now try the bug from before. `word` is a shared borrow of `s`, and `s.clear()` needs a mutable borrow while `word` is still used. The borrowing rules from the last lesson forbid exactly that, so the compiler catches the bug:

blocks.explain: `s.find(' ')` returns the byte index of the first space, or `None`; `unwrap_or(s.len())` uses the full length when there is no space. It is a shorter way to write the loop above.

blocks.title: String literals are slices
blocks.md:
Remember `let s = "Hello, world!";`? The type of `s` is `&str`: a slice pointing to text stored inside the program's binary. That is why literals are immutable: `&str` is a shared reference.

This also means a function that takes `&str` can accept both literals and Strings, because a `&String` converts to a `&str` automatically (this is called **deref coercion**, chapter 15). So the better signature for `first_word` is:

```rust
fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str
```

blocks.title: &str versus String
blocks.md: `String` owns growable text on the heap. `&str` borrows some text that lives elsewhere: in a String, in the binary, anywhere. Store `String` in your data; take `&str` as a parameter when you only read text. This is one of the most common pairs of types you will use.

blocks.title: Write last_word
blocks.md: Write `last_word`, returning a slice of everything after the last space (or the whole text when there is no space). `rfind` is like `find` but searches from the end. The program should print the three lines in the task.
hints: `s.rfind(' ')` returns `Some(index)` of the last space, or `None`.
The word starts one byte after the space: `&s[i + 1..]`. Use `match` as in the guessing game, or `if let Some(i) = s.rfind(' ')`.

blocks.title: Other slices
blocks.md: Slices are not just for text. A slice of an array (or, later, a `Vec`) has type `&[T]`, and `&mut [T]` is a slice you can change. Functions that take `&[T]` work for arrays of any length, which plain arrays cannot do because the length is part of their type.

cards.back: Owned, growable UTF-8 text on the heap.
A borrowed string slice: pointer + length into text owned elsewhere. String literals have this type.
A borrowed slice of elements of type T, from an array, a Vec or another slice.
A mutable slice: lets a function change elements, but not add or remove them.
A slice of bytes 2, 3 and 4 of `s`.
Cannot borrow as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable: a shared borrow is still in use.

blocks.title: Slicing text and numbers
blocks.goal: Write functions that take and return slices, so they work on Strings, literals, arrays and parts of them.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str`: everything before the first space (the whole text if there is none).
- `pub fn nth_word(s: &str, n: usize) -> Option<&str>`: the n-th word (0-based) when words are separated by single spaces, or `None` if there are fewer words.
- `pub fn largest(values: &[i32]) -> Option<i32>`: the largest value, or `None` for an empty slice.
- `pub fn zero_negatives(values: &mut [i32])`: replace every negative number with 0, in place.
hints: `nth_word`: `s.split(' ')` gives the words one by one; count them in a `for` loop with a counter, and `return Some(word)` when the counter equals `n`. After the loop, `None`.
`largest`: return `None` if `values.is_empty()`, else start from `values[0]` and loop.
blocks.solution_explain: Every function borrows, so callers keep ownership and can pass whole collections or parts of them. `for &v in values` destructures each `&i32` into an `i32`. Later chapters replace these loops with iterator methods such as `s.split(' ').nth(n)` and `values.iter().max()`.

questions.explanation: Bytes 4 to the end: r-u-s-t are 0 to 3, so the slice starts at `a`.

questions.q: What is the type of the literal `"hi"`?
questions.explanation: A string literal is a slice of text stored in the binary.

questions.q: Why is `fn f(s: &str)` usually better than `fn f(s: &String)`?
options: It accepts both literals and Strings (and slices of them)
questions.explanation: A `&String` coerces to `&str`, but not the other way round, so `&str` accepts more.

questions.q: Holding a slice of a String while calling `clear()` on that String compiles, and the slice becomes empty.
questions.explanation: The slice is a shared borrow; `clear` needs a mutable one. The compiler reports E0502.

questions.q: Which signature lets a function sum arrays of **any** length?
questions.explanation: A slice type has no length in it, so any array (or part of one) fits.

options: Panics: byte index 2 is not a char boundary
questions.explanation: Byte 2 falls inside `é` (bytes 1 and 2), and string slices must start and end on character boundaries.

points: A slice borrows a contiguous part of a collection: `&s[a..b]`, `&s[..b]`, `&s[a..]`, `&s[..]`.
`&str` is a string slice; string literals are `&str`.
Returning a slice ties it to its source, so the borrow checker catches uses after the source changes.
Prefer `&str` parameters to `&String`, and `&[T]` to `&[T; N]` or `&Vec<T>`.
String slice indexes are byte positions and must fall on character boundaries.
`&mut [T]` lets a function change elements in place.

terms.def: A reference to a contiguous sequence of elements in a collection: a pointer and a length.
A string slice: borrowed UTF-8 text. String literals have this type.
Automatic conversion of a reference to another reference type, such as &String to &str.
